title: Rashi on the Talmud
hookLine: Rashi explains word by word; without him most learners would be lost

cards: A first-time learner is stuck on one Aramaic word. The line runs on with hardly a pause, and nothing says who is speaking. The page feels like a locked door.
A teacher leans over and taps the narrow column at the inside of the page. Start there. Don't read it all.
Just find the note on the word you're stuck on. You find it: a few words copied from the text, then a short, plain sentence. The door opens a crack.

teach.b: Rashi on the Talmud. You've heard Rashi's name since year one. It's formed from the initials of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, a teacher in medieval France, in the town of Troyes.
He wrote commentary on the Torah and on the Talmud, and his Talmud commentary is the one printed in the inner margin. First, how it works.
Each comment opens with a few words copied from the Gemara, a heading, so you can match it to the spot you're stuck on.

teach.h: A HEADING, THEN A SHORT NOTE.
teach.b: Then comes a short explanation: what this word means, who is speaking, what the question is. He moves with the text, line by line, rarely stopping to argue. Second, what he does for an argument.
Back on the first page of Berakhot, the evening Shema, Rashi pauses on a practice of his own day: people recited the Shema in the synagogue before dark. So how does that fit the mishnah's time?

He explains that the evening service is said to stand in prayer out of words of Torah, and that the main duty is fulfilled by the Shema said at bedtime. A short note, and suddenly the text touches a real evening.
Sometimes Rashi glosses a hard word with a word in the French of his day, written in Hebrew letters, so some scholars now read him for old French as well.
Some learners say that without Rashi the Talmud would stay closed to them. He doesn't argue with the text. He walks beside you through it.

how: Talmud learners read Rashi's commentary alongside the Gemara, matching each comment's heading words to the line they are studying; in a class, the teacher often reads the Gemara and Rashi together, line by line.

games.q: what does “rashi on the talmud” mean?
o: the commentary in the inner margin, explaining word by word
a summary of the law printed at the end of each tractate
a short prayer said before opening a page of Talmud

games.q: Rashi on the Talmud — tap the pairs.
p: the town in France where he taught

s: Rashi's commentary argues with the Gemara at every turn
he walks beside the text, explaining words and moves, rarely stopping to argue.
each Rashi comment opens with words copied from the Gemara
a heading, so you can match the note to the spot you're stuck on.
Rashi wrote only on the Talmud
he wrote commentary on the Torah and on the Talmud.

games.q: people in your community recite the evening Shema in the synagogue while it's still light. the mishnah's time hasn't come yet. you're Rashi, writing your note. what do you explain?
o: that the synagogue practice is simply wrong.
that the service stands prayer on words of Torah, and the main duty is the Shema at bedtime.
that the time in the mishnah doesn't matter.
games.why: Rashi explains the early recital as a way to stand in prayer out of words of Torah, with the main duty fulfilled by the bedtime Shema. a short note that touches a real evening.

practice: Picture the narrow column at the inside of the page: a heading, from when, and then the note that the main duty is the Shema at bedtime. Let that land in your own evening, and ask where you end your day.
On the breath in, from when; on the breath out, at bedtime.

wordCard.voice: Rashi on the Talmud. The commentary in the inner margin that explains the Gemara word by word, heading by heading. Today's word.
